claim: Allosteric HIV-1 integrase (IN) inhibitors (ALLINIs) are a promising new class of antiretroviral agents that disrupt proper viral maturation by inducing hyper-multimerization of IN.
source: Allosteric HIV-1 integrase (IN) inhibitors (ALLINIs) are a promising new class of antiretroviral agents that disrupt proper viral maturation by inducing hyper-multimerization of IN.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract that references the established mechanism of ALLINIs, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Lead pyridine-based ALLINI KF116 exhibits striking selectivity for IN tetramers versus lower order protein oligomers.
source: Here we show that lead pyridine-based ALLINI KF116 exhibits striking selectivity for IN tetramers versus lower order protein oligomers.
evidence: This claim is supported by DLS experiments shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, demonstrating that KF116 induces higher-order multimerization of tetramers but not dimers or monomers.

claim: IN structural features that are essential for its functional tetramerization and HIV-1 replication are also critically important for KF116 mediated higher-order IN multimerization.
source: IN structural features that are essential for its functional tetramerization and HIV-1 replication are also critically important for KF116 mediated higher-order IN multimerization.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments in Figure 4 showing that mutations affecting tetramerization (H12A, K14A, Y15A, etc.) also affect KF116-induced multimerization.

claim: KF116 treatment during virion production compromises the tight association of IN with capsid cores during subsequent infection of target cells.
source: Live cell imaging of single viral particles revealed that KF116 treatment during virion production compromises the tight association of IN with capsid cores during subsequent infection of target cells.
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data in Figure 8 showing loss of INmNG signal from CypA-DsRed labeled cores in KF116-treated viruses.

claim: The highly active (-)-KF116 enantiomer displayed EC50 of ~7 nM against wild type HIV-1.
source: We have synthesized the highly active (-)-KF116 enantiomer, which displayed EC50 of ~7 nM against wild type HIV-1
evidence: This is directly supported by antiviral activity data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: (-)-KF116 displayed ~10 fold higher, sub-nM activity against a clinically relevant dolutegravir resistant mutant virus.
source: which displayed EC50 of ~7 nM against wild type HIV-1 and ~10 fold higher, sub-nM activity against a clinically relevant dolutegravir resistant mutant virus
evidence: This is supported by antiviral activity data in Figure 7B showing enhanced activity against HIV-1 containing IN N155H/K156N/K211R/E212T substitutions.

claim: Clinical applications of first generation INSTIs raltegravir (RAL) and elvitegravir (EVG) resulted in evolution of drug resistant phenotypes containing IN substitutions in the vicinity of the inhibitor binding sites.
source: Clinical applications of first generation INSTIs raltegravir (RAL) and elvitegravir (EVG) resulted in evolution of drug resistant phenotypes containing IN substitutions in the vicinity of the inhibitor binding sites (Cooper et al., 2008; Garrido et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on INSTI resistance.

claim: Second generation dolutegravir (DTG), bictegravir (BIC) and investigational drug cabotegravir (CAB) exhibit significantly higher genetic pressure for the evolution of drug resistance.
source: Second generation dolutegravir (DTG), bictegravir (BIC) and investigational drug cabotegravir (CAB) exhibit significantly higher genetic pressure for the evolution of drug resistance and yield complex resistance pathways with IN substitutions in both the proximity of and significantly distanced from inhibitor binding sites (Cahn et al., 2013; Eron et al., 2013; Malet et al., 2018; Margolis et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2018; Tsiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature on second-generation INSTI resistance.

claim: ALLINIs are highly potent during virion maturation.
source: Unlike INSTIs, ALLINIs are highly potent during virion maturation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and is consistent with the mechanism described throughout the manuscript.

claim: ALLINIs induce higher-order IN multimerization in virions and consequently inhibit IN-RNA interactions.
source: They induce higher-order IN multimerization in virions and consequently inhibit IN-RNA interactions, which in turn yields eccentric noninfectious virions with the ribonucleoprotein complexes (RNPs) mislocalized outside of the translucent capsid (CA) cores (Balakrishnan et al., 2013; Desimmie et al., 2013; Fontana et al., 2015; Gupta et al., 2014; Jurado et al., 2013; Kessl et al., 2016; van Bel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature describing ALLINI mechanism of action.

claim: ALLINIs display a secondary, albeit significantly reduced, activity during early steps of HIV-1 infection where these compounds interfere with HIV-1 IN binding to its cognate cellular cofactor LEDGF/p75.
source: ALLINIs also display a secondary, albeit significantly reduced, activity during early steps of HIV-1 infection where these compounds interfere with HIV-1 IN binding to its cognate cellular cofactor LEDGF/p75 (Christ and Debyser, 2013; Christ et al., 2012; Christ et al., 2010; Kessl et al., 2012; Le Rouzic et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2014; Tsiang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature on ALLINI activity during early infection.

claim: The key pharmacophore in all potent ALLINIs includes both a carboxylic acid and tert-butoxy group, which extend from a core aromatic ring system.
source: The key pharmacophore in all potent ALLINIs includes both a carboxylic acid and tert-butoxy group, which extend from a core aromatic ring system (Figure 1A) (Christ et al., 2010; Jurado and Engelman, 2013; Sharma et al., 2014; Tsiang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and is illustrated in Figure 1A showing the chemical structures of KF116 and BI224436.

claim: The original series of compounds contained a quinoline core, exhibited relatively modest potency, and comparatively low genetic barrier to drug resistance.
source: The original series of compounds contained a quinoline core, exhibited relatively modest potency, and comparatively low genetic barrier to drug resistance (Christ et al., 2010; Fader et al., 2014b; Feng et al., 2013; Tsiang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on quinoline-based ALLINIs.

claim: BI224436 exhibits antiviral EC50 of ~14 nM.
source: efforts that retain the quinoline core while varying the substituted groups have resulted in highly potent inhibitors such as BI224436 with antiviral EC50 of ~14 nM (Fader et al., 2014b) (Figure 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Pyridine-based compounds exhibit markedly improved antiviral activities and significantly enhanced genetic pressure for the evolution of resistance compared with archetypal quinoline-based compounds.
source: We and others have rationally developed pyridine-based compounds that exhibit markedly improved antiviral activities and significantly enhanced genetic pressure for the evolution of resistance compared with archetypal quinoline-based compounds (Fader et al., 2016; Hoyte et al., 2017; Sharma et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature including the authors' own work.

claim: Racemic pyridine-based compound KF116 exhibited ~24 nM antiviral activity.
source: For example, our lead racemic pyridine-based compound, KF116 (Figure 1A), exhibited ~24 nM antiviral activity
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the authors' previous work (Sharma et al., 2014).

claim: KF116 remained fully potent with respect to A128T IN mutant virus that confers significant resistance to archetypal quinoline-based ALLINIs.
source: and remained fully potent with respect to A128T IN mutant virus that confers significant resistance to archetypal quinoline-based ALLINIs.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the authors' previous work.

claim: Triple IN substitutions (T124N/V165I/T174I), which substantially compromise viral replication, were needed to confer effective resistance to KF116.
source: Instead, triple IN substitutions (T124N/V165I/T174I), which substantially compromise viral replication, were needed to confer effective resistance to KF116 (Hoyte et al., 2017; Sharma et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: Extensive in vitro ADME and animal pharmacokinetic studies of quinoline- and pyridine-based inhibitors performed by Boehringer Ingelheim have indicated the superiority of the pyridine-based compounds as 'a clinically viable starting point'.
source: Furthermore, extensive in vitro absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) and animal pharmacokinetic studies of quinoline- and pyridine-based inhibitors performed by Boehringer Ingelheim (BI) have indicated the superiority of the pyridine-based compounds as 'a clinically viable starting point' (Fader et al., 2016; Fader et al., 2014a; Fenwick et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature from Boehringer Ingelheim.

claim: HIV-1 IN is comprised of three structurally distinct domains: N-terminal domain (NTD), catalytic core domain (CCD) and C-terminal domain (CTD).
source: IN is comprised of three structurally distinct domains: N-terminal domain (NTD), catalytic core domain (CCD) and C-terminal domain (CTD) (Chiu and Davies, 2004; Engelman and Cherepanov, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV-1 IN structure, supported by citations.

claim: Biochemical and x-ray crystallography experiments with individual domains revealed that ALLINIs selectively bind to a v-shaped pocket located at the CCD dimer interface.
source: Biochemical and x-ray crystallography experiments with individual domains revealed that ALLINIs selectively bind to a v-shaped pocket located at the CCD dimer interface (Fader et al., 2014b; Feng et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published structural studies.

claim: The ALLINI core rings do not directly interact with IN but enable the conserved pharmacophore carboxylic acid and tert-butoxy groups to accurately position within the v-shaped pocket.
source: Mechanistic studies with various ALLINI core ring structures have shown that the cores do not directly interact with IN. Instead, they enable the conserved pharmacophore carboxylic acid and tert-butoxy groups to accurately position within the v-shaped pocket allowing hydrogen bonding with backbone amides of IN residues Glu-170 and His-171 and the side chain of Thr-174, respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on mechanistic studies and describes the binding mode of ALLINIs.

claim: Mass spectrometry-based protein foot-printing experiments with full-length IN identified that in addition to the CCD, the CTD plays a critical role for inhibitor induced hyper-multimerization of IN.
source: Mass spectrometry-based protein foot-printing experiments (Feng et al., 2016; Shkriabai et al., 2014) with full-length IN identified that in addition to the CCD, the CTD plays a critical role for inhibitor induced hyper-multimerization of IN.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published mass spectrometry studies.

claim: Molecular modeling studies suggested that ALLINIs directly promote inter‐subunit interactions between the CCD dimer and the CTD of another IN dimer.
source: In turn, these findings enabled molecular modeling studies, which suggested that ALLINIs directly promote inter‐subunit interactions between the CCD dimer and the CTD of another IN dimer (Deng et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published modeling study.

claim: Free energy calculations revealed that in the absence of the inhibitor the v-shaped binding cavity on the CCD dimer is occupied with thermodynamically unstable water.
source: Furthermore, free energy calculations revealed that in the absence of the inhibitor the v-shaped binding cavity on the CCD dimer is occupied with thermodynamically unstable water, which minimizes potential CCD-CTD interactions.
evidence: This claim is based on computational free energy calculations, likely from the cited Deng et al., 2016 study.

claim: ALLINI binding to the CCD dimer effectively fills the v-shaped pocket by displacing the water molecules and thus markedly enhances the binding interface for incoming CTD.
source: In contrast, ALLINI binding to the CCD dimer effectively fills the v-shaped pocket by displacing the water molecules and thus markedly enhances the binding interface for incoming CTD.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling and free energy calculations.

claim: The crystal structure of full-length HIV-1 IN Y15A/F185H in complex with quinoline-based ALLINI GSK1264 revealed two IN Y15A/F185H dimers bridged by two quinoline-based GSK1264 inhibitors through head (CCD-CCD dimer) to tail (CTD of another dimer) interactions.
source: More recently, the crystal structure of full-length HIV-1 IN Y15A/F185H in complex with quinoline-based ALLINI GSK1264 was reported (Gupta et al., 2016), which confirmed both the earlier biochemical results and predicted model of a multimer interface involving CCD-inhibitor-CTD interactions. The crystal structure revealed two IN Y15A/F185H dimers bridged by two quinoline-based GSK1264 inhibitors through head (CCD-CCD dimer) to tail (CTD of another dimer) interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the published crystal structure.

claim: KF116 specifically induced higher-order oligomerization of tetramers but not dimers or monomers.
source: The results in Figure 1C show that KF116 specifically induced higher-order oligomerization of tetramers but not dimers or monomers.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by DLS data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Within 1 min after addition of KF116 to IN tetramers, higher-order protein multimers with particle diameter sizes of ~200 nm were formed.
source: More detailed kinetic analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) revealed that within 1 min after addition of KF116 to IN tetramers, higher-order protein multimers with particle diameter sizes of ~200 nm were formed.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic DLS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Particle diameter sizes increased further to ~1,000 nm in a time dependent manner indicating an equilibrium shift towards higher-order multimers.
source: Particle diameter sizes increased further to ~1,000 nm in a time dependent manner indicating an equilibrium shift towards higher-order multimers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic DLS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: KF116 failed to alter the multimeric form of dimers or monomers even after a 60 min incubation.
source: In sharp contrast, the inhibitor failed to alter the multimeric form of dimers or monomers even after a 60 min incubation (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by DLS data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: BI224436 exhibited a broader specificity for tetramers and dimers but did not have any effects on IN monomers.
source: In parallel reactions, we have analyzed the quinoline-based BI224436, which exhibited a broader specificity for tetramers and dimers but did not have any effects on IN monomers (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by DLS data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: Addition of BI224436 to IN tetramers yielded higher-order multimers within 1 min.
source: Addition of BI224436 to IN tetramers yielded higher-order multimers within 1 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic DLS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A longer incubation time (at least 30 min) for BI224436 +IN dimers was needed to detect higher-order IN multimers.
source: whereas a longer incubation time (at least 30 min) for BI224436 +IN dimers was needed to detect higher-order IN multimers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic DLS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The stoichiometry for KF116:IN is 2:4 suggesting that two molecules of KF116 bridge two IN tetramers.
source: The results in Figure 2 indicate a 2:4 ratio for KF116:IN suggesting that two molecules of KF116 bridge two IN tetramers.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative aggregation data shown in Figure 2.

claim: BI224436:IN interactions exhibited a 2:2 or 4:4 ratio.
source: In contrast, BI224436:IN interactions exhibited a 2:2 or 4:4 ratio (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), similar to the prior crystal structure (Gupta et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative aggregation data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: KF116 and BI224436 promoted higher-order multimerization of only full-length IN, whereas all truncated protein constructs (CCD, NTD-CCD and CCD-CTD) exhibited marked resistance.
source: DLS results in Figure 3A and B, show that KF116 and BI224436 promoted higher-order multimerization of only full-length IN, whereas all truncated protein constructs (CCD, NTD-CCD and CCD-CTD) exhibited marked resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by DLS data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Addition of KF116 or BI224436 aggregated full-length WT IN in a dose dependent manner, whereas the CCD and NTD-CCD, both of which lacked the CTD, remained fully soluble even after incubation with 20 µM inhibitors.
source: Addition of KF116 or BI224436 aggregated full-length WT IN in a dose dependent manner, whereas the CCD and NTD-CCD, both of which lacked the CTD, remained fully soluble even after incubation with 20 µM inhibitors (Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by aggregation assay data shown in Figure 3C, D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The CCD-CTD, which contained all inhibitor interacting interfaces but which lacked the NTD, exhibited substantial resistance to both KF116 and BI224436 induced aggregation.
source: Interestingly, the CCD-CTD, which contained all inhibitor interacting interfaces but which lacked the NTD, also exhibited substantial resistance to both KF116 and BI224436 induced aggregation (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by aggregation assay data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Only residual aggregation of CCD-CTD was detected at higher KF116 and BI224436 concentrations (>10 µM), whereas these inhibitor concentrations fully precipitated full-length WT IN.
source: Of note, only residual aggregation of CCD-CTD was detected at higher KF116 and BI224436 concentrations (>10 µM), whereas these inhibitor concentrations fully precipitated full-length WT IN.
evidence: This claim is supported by aggregation assay data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: In addition to the CCD and CTD, the NTD is critically important for the inhibitor induced higher-order IN multimerization.
source: Collectively, these findings (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) indicate that in addition to the CCD and CTD, the NTD is critically important for the inhibitor induced higher-order IN multimerization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 3 showing that CCD-CTD lacking NTD is resistant to ALLINI-induced aggregation.

claim: The NTD does not directly interact with the inhibitors but this domain is essential for functional tetramerization of IN.
source: Unlike the CCD and CTD, the NTD does not directly interact with the inhibitors but this domain is essential for functional tetramerization of IN (Hare et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published structural studies.

claim: The NTD from one dimer engages with the CCD of another dimer to help form stable tetramers.
source: Specifically, the NTD from one dimer engages with the CCD of another dimer to help form stable tetramers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IN tetramerization, supported by citation to Hare et al., 2009.

claim: The NTD interacts with the α-helical linker (200-222) connecting the CCD with the CTD.
source: In addition, the NTD interacts with the α-helical linker (200-222) connecting the CCD with the CTD.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge and is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The H12A IN substitution markedly altered IN oligomerization, yielding a mixture of monomers and higher-order oligomers.
source: The H12A IN substitution, which destabilizes binding of the architecturally important Zn2+, markedly altered IN oligomerization, yielding a mixture of monomers and higher-order oligomers (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: H12A IN was susceptible to BI224436 but exhibited marked resistance to KF116.
source: H12A IN was susceptible to BI224436 but exhibited marked resistance to KF116 (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by DLS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The K14A change destabilized NTD-CCD interactions needed for functional IN tetramerization and resulted in IN dimers.
source: The K14A change destabilized NTD-CCD interactions needed for functional IN tetramerization and resulted in IN dimers (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: KF116 was completely inactive against K14A IN, whereas BI224436 remained active.
source: KF116 was completely inactive, whereas BI224436 remained active against K14A IN (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by DLS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Y15A IN, which yielded a mixture of dimers and monomers, was resistant to both KF116 and BI224436.
source: Y15A IN, which yielded a mixture of dimers and monomers, was resistant to both KF116 and BI224436.
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC and DLS data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Y15A/F185H IN, which yielded dimers, was susceptible to quinoline-based BI224436 but this mutant was completely resistant to pyridine-based KF116.
source: Y15A/F185H IN, which was utilized in the x-ray structure with quinoline-based compounds (Gupta et al., 2016) and which yielded dimers, was susceptible to quinoline-based BI224436 but this mutant was completely resistant to pyridine-based KF116 (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC and DLS data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: T210 +Pro IN was completely resistant to both KF116 and BI224436 indicating that the linear α-helix is critically important for accurate orientation of the CCD-inhibitor-CTD interfaces.
source: T210 +Pro IN was completely resistant to both KF116 and BI224436 indicating that the linear α-helix is critically important for accurate orientation of the CCD-inhibitor-CTD interfaces.
evidence: This claim is supported by DLS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and represents an interpretation of the results.

claim: Deletion of A205 within the α-helix rendered IN resistant to both KF116 and BI224436.
source: Similarly, deletion of A205 within the α-helix rendered IN resistant to both KF116 and BI224436.
evidence: This claim is supported by DLS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The substitutions in the NTD or the CCD-CTD connecting α-helix impaired virus infectivity and inhibited IN catalytic activity in vitro.
source: The substitutions in the NTD or the CCD-CTD connecting α-helix, both of which compromised functional tetramerization of IN, also impaired virus infectivity and inhibited IN catalytic activity in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4) (Hare et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: The substitutions in the NTD or the CCD-CTD connecting α-helix adversely affected LEDGF/p75 binding with lesser effects seen for the T210 +Pro substitution.
source: Furthermore, these substitutions also adversely affected LEDGF/p75 binding with lesser effects seen for the T210 +Pro substitution, which is significantly distanced from LEDGF/p75 binding sites in the NTD or CCD (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by LEDGF/p75 binding data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The control N222K substitution in the CCD-CTD connecting α-helix formed tetramers, retained WT levels of HIV-1 replication in cell culture, IN catalytic activity and LEDGF/p75 binding in vitro, and was fully susceptible to both KF116 and BI224436 induced higher-order IN multimerization.
source: The control N222K substitution in the CCD-CTD connecting α-helix formed tetramers, retained WT levels of HIV-1 replication in cell culture, IN catalytic activity and LEDGF/p75 binding in vitro, and was fully susceptible to both KF116 and BI224436 induced higher-order IN multimerization (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–4.

claim: An ionic bond between E11 in the NTD of one dimer and K186 within the CCD of another dimer is important for functional tetramerization of IN.
source: Published structural studies (Hare et al., 2009) have revealed key interactions that govern IN tetramerization. For example, an ionic bond between E11 in the NTD of one dimer and K186 within the CCD of another dimer is important for functional tetramerization of IN (Hare et al., 2009) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published structural studies and is illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: Individual E11K and K186E IN substitutions fully compromise protein tetramerization (without affecting IN dimerization) due to charge-charge repulsions.
source: Individual E11K and K186E IN substitutions fully compromise protein tetramerization (without affecting IN dimerization) due to charge-charge repulsions.
evidence: This claim is based on published structural studies (Hare et al., 2009) and is supported by the trans-complementation experiments.

claim: Mixing two mutant proteins (E11K and K186E INs) in vitro allows for partial reconstitution of functional IN tetramers through reversed charge-charge interactions.
source: However, mixing two mutant proteins (E11K and K186E INs) in vitro allows for partial reconstitution of functional IN tetramers through reversed charge-charge interactions (Hare et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Hare et al., 2009) and is confirmed by the authors' own data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Individual E11K and K186E substitutions compromised the catalytic activities of IN and its ability to bind LEDGF/p75, whereas these functions of IN were substantially restored through reconstituting the two inactive proteins (E11K + K186E INs).
source: Indeed, the results in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 show that individual E11K and K186E substitutions compromised the catalytic activities of IN and its ability to bind LEDGF/p75, whereas these functions of IN were substantially restored through reconstituting the two inactive proteins (E11K + K186E INs).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of KF116 to either E11K or K186E IN dimers did not induce higher-order protein multimerization.
source: DLS results in Figure 5B revealed that addition of KF116 to either E11K or K186E IN dimers did not induce higher-order protein multimerization.
evidence: This claim is supported by DLS data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When two resistant IN mutants (E11K and K186E) were mixed together to allow reconstitution of IN tetramers and then incubated with KF116, formation of higher-order protein multimers was observed.
source: However, when two resistant IN mutants (E11K and K186E) were mixed together to allow reconstitution of IN tetramers and then incubated with KF116 under identical reaction conditions, we observed formation of higher-order protein multimers (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by DLS data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: BI224436 induced higher-order multimerization of dimeric K186E and reconstituted tetrameric E11K + K186E INs.
source: In parallel experiments, BI224436 induced higher-order multimerization of dimeric K186E and reconstituted tetrameric E11K + K186E INs (Figure 5C)
evidence: This claim is supported by DLS data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: E11K IN was resistant to BI224436 suggesting that this substitution, in addition to destabilizing IN tetramers, could also potentially affect the proper orientation of the NTD required for BI224436 induced higher-order IN multimerization of the IN dimers.
source: However, E11K IN was resistant to BI224436 suggesting that this substitution, in addition to destabilizing IN tetramers, could also potentially affect the proper orientation of the NTD required for BI224436 induced higher-order IN multimerization of the IN dimers.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DLS data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: E11K was significantly more defective for IN catalytic activity than was K186E IN.
source: Accordingly, we also note that E11K was significantly more defective for IN catalytic activity than was K186E IN (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by catalytic activity data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HADDOCK docking simulations generated top ranked symmetric head-to-tail architecture, with the two tetramers connected by two CCD-KF116-CTD interfaces.
source: Docking simulations using HADDOCK generated top ranked symmetric head-to-tail architecture, with the two tetramers connected by two CCD-KF116-CTD interfaces (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is based on computational docking simulations using HADDOCK.

claim: The KF116 model is fully consistent with the experimentally observed stoichiometry of 2:4 for KF116:IN.
source: This model is fully consistent with the experimentally observed stoichiometry of 2:4 for KF116:IN.
evidence: This is a statement connecting the modeling results to the experimental stoichiometry data from Figure 2.

claim: The KF116 mediated buried surface area (BSA) between two tetramers was ~2000 Å2–3200 Å2.
source: The KF116 mediated buried surface area (BSA) between two tetramers was ~2000 Å2–3200 Å2.
evidence: This is a result from the molecular modeling calculations.

claim: When IN dimers instead of tetramers were used as building blocks, the HADDOCK program failed to yield symmetric dimer:KF116:dimer assemblies.
source: Strikingly, when we used IN dimers instead of tetramers as building blocks, the HADDOCK program failed to yield symmetric dimer:KF116:dimer assemblies.
evidence: This is a result from the molecular modeling calculations.

claim: The carboxylic acid moiety of BI224436 maintains important hydrogen bonding interactions with the backbone amides of E170 and H171.
source: In common with all other potent ALLINIs, the carboxylic acid moiety of BI224436 maintains important hydrogen bonding interactions with the backbone amides of E170 and H171.
evidence: This claim is based on the crystal structure of BI224436 bound to IN CCD shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The hydrogen bonding interaction of the ether oxygen of the tert-butoxy and the side chain of T174 is conserved in BI224436.
source: In addition, the hydrogen bonding interaction of the ether oxygen of the tert-butoxy and the side chain of T174 is conserved.
evidence: This claim is based on the crystal structure of BI224436 bound to IN CCD shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The bulky nature of the tricyclic ring of BI224436 fully fills the hydrophobic pocket of the CCD dimer and extends closer to W132.
source: However, there are the following important differences between BI224436 and KF116 binding (Figure 6C): i) the bulky nature of the tricyclic ring of BI224436 fully fills the hydrophobic pocket of the CCD dimer and extends closer to W132, which caps the pocket.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of crystal structures shown in Figure 6C.

claim: KF116 contains a much smaller benzyl substitution at the position where BI224436 has a bulky tricyclic ring.
source: For comparison, KF116 contains a much smaller benzyl substitution at this position
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of crystal structures shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The benzimidazole group, which is both unique and essential for KF116 activity, projects outside of the v-shaped pocket, whereas BI224436 is more deeply positioned within the pocket.
source: ii) the benzimidazole group, which is both unique and essential for KF116 activity, projects outside of the v-shaped pocket, whereas BI224436 is more deeply positioned within the pocket.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of crystal structures shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Symmetric multimers can be generated with BI224436 regardless of whether IN tetramers or dimers are used as building blocks.
source: Symmetric multimers can be generated regardless of whether IN tetramers or dimers are used as building blocks suggesting that unlike KF116, BI224436 can recruit both tetramers and dimers for higher-order IN multimerization.
evidence: This is a result from the molecular modeling calculations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: (-)-KF116 exhibited an IC50 of ~7 nM, which was ~30 times more potent than its (+) counterpart.
source: (-)-KF116 exhibited an IC50 of ~7 nM, which was ~30 times more potent than its (+) counterpart (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by antiviral activity data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: (-)-KF116 displayed excellent metabolic stability toward CYP oxidation with superior properties compared with racemic KF116 and quinoline-based BI224436.
source: ALLINIs displayed excellent metabolic stability toward CYP oxidation with (-)-KF116 exhibiting superior properties compared with racemic KF116 and quinoline-based BI224436.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolic stability data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A recent clinical study revealed that failure of DTG treatment in patients was observed with concomitant appearance of IN N155H/K211R/E212T substitutions on the background of the K156N polymorphic mutation.
source: For example, a recent clinical study revealed that failure of DTG treatment in patients was observed with concomitant appearance of IN N155H/K211R/E212T substitutions on the background of the K156N polymorphic mutation (Malet et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published clinical study.

claim: KF116 displayed sub-nM activity and was ~10 fold more active against HIV-1 containing IN N155H/K156N/K211R/E212T substitutions compared with the WT virus.
source: Interestingly, KF116 displayed sub-nM activity and was ~10 fold more active against HIV-1 containing IN N155H/K156N/K211R/E212T substitutions compared with the WT virus (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by antiviral activity data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: KF116 was similarly active against WT HIV-1 and the mutant virus containing only the CCD (N155H/K156N) substitutions.
source: In control assays, KF116 was similarly active against WT HIV-1 and the mutant virus containing only the CCD (N155H/K156N) substitutions (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by antiviral activity data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Recombinant IN(N155H/K156N/K211R/E212T) is almost exclusively tetramer, whereas IN(N155H/K156N) forms a mixture of tetramers, dimers and monomers.
source: Our SEC data (Figure 7C) show that recombinant IN(N155H/K156N/K211R/E212T) is almost exclusively tetramer, whereas IN(N155H/K156N), which is similar to WT IN (Figure 7C), forms a mixture of tetramers, dimers and monomers.
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Imaging of single viral complexes bound to a cover glass before or after 5 min of virus entry into target cells showed similar extents of colocalization between CypA-DsRed and INmNG puncta in all samples.
source: Imaging of single viral complexes bound to a cover glass before or after 5 min of virus entry into target cells showed similar extents of colocalization between CypA-DsRed and INmNG puncta in all samples (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Imaging of virions at 90 min post-infection revealed a marked drop in the number of co-labeled particles (primarily due to a loss of IN signal) for viruses produced in the presence of ALLINIs, but not for control viruses prepared in the presence of DMSO or RAL.
source: However, imaging of these virions in the same target cells at 90 min post-infection revealed a marked drop in the number of co-labeled particles (primarily due to a loss of IN signal) for viruses produced in the presence of ALLINIs, but not for control viruses prepared in the presence of DMSO or RAL (Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: DMSO-treated control viruses undergo uncoating manifested in a loss of CypA-DsRed from INmNG labeled complexes.
source: Single particle tracking revealed that DMSO-treated control viruses undergo uncoating manifested in a loss of CypA-DsRed from INmNG labeled complexes (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by single particle tracking data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: A gradual decay of the INmNG signal was observed after the loss of CypA-DsRed signal from the viral complexes produced in the presence of the control DMSO solvent.
source: In agreement with our previous studies showing proteasomal degradation of post-uncoating IN complexes in the cytoplasm (Francis et al., 2016; Francis and Melikyan, 2018), we observed a gradual decay of the INmNG signal after the loss of CypA-DsRed signal from the viral complexes produced in the presence of the control DMSO solvent (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by single particle tracking data shown in Figure 8C and citations to previous studies.

claim: ALLINI treated virions lost the INmNG signal prior to the loss of CypA-DsRed/CA.
source: In contrast, ALLINI treated virions lost the INmNG signal prior to the loss of CypA-DsRed/CA (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by single particle tracking data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: ALLINI induced INmNG aggregates are readily accessible to proteasomal degradation in the cytoplasm of target cells due likely to their mislocalization outside of the protective CA cores.
source: These findings suggest that ALLINI induced INmNG aggregates are readily accessible to proteasomal degradation in the cytoplasm of target cells due likely to their mislocalization outside of the protective CA cores (Figure 8—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the imaging data, combining observations with inference about the mechanism.

claim: BI224436 is positioned deeper inside the v-shaped pocket compared to KF116.
source: BI224436 (similarly to its very close analog GSK1264) is positioned deeper inside the v-shaped pocket (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is inferred from the crystal structure comparison shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The bulky benzimidazole group of KF116 could force the incoming CTD to accept a slightly different orientation compared to BI224436 or GSK1264.
source: In contrast, the bulky benzimidazole group, which is both unique and essential for KF116 activity, extends from the v-shaped pocket (Figure 6C) and could force the incoming CTD to accept a slightly different orientation compared to BI224436 or GSK1264.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural differences observed in Figure 6C.

claim: The different orientation of CTD imposed by KF116 may hamper the dimer-dimer symmetry seen with GSK1264 but instead optimally position two IN tetramers for symmetrical CCD-KF116-CTD interactions.
source: This, in turn may hamper the dimer-dimer symmetry seen with GSK1264 (Gupta et al., 2016) but instead optimally position two IN tetramers for symmetrical CCD-KF116-CTD interactions (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting structural observations to the differential oligomer specificity.

claim: The NTD effectively stabilizes the conformation of the CCD-CTD α-helical linker as well as the entire tetramer against thermal fluctuations through dual interactions with the CCD-CTD α-helical linker and the CCD of another dimer unit.
source: Within each IN tetramer, the NTD interacts with the CCD-CTD α-helical linker as well as the CCD of another dimer unit. These dual interactions allow the NTD to effectively stabilize the conformation of the CCD-CTD α-helical linker as well as the entire tetramer against thermal fluctuations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural interactions observed in the models and the mutagenesis data.

claim: Conformational rigidity of IN tetramers could facilitate symmetric tetramer-ALLINI-tetramer assemblies.
source: In turn, such conformational rigidity could facilitate symmetric tetramer-ALLINI-tetramer assemblies.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the structural stability to the ability to form symmetric assemblies.

claim: The predominant form of IN in virions resides as a tetramer.
source: Since both KF116 and BI224436 are highly potent during virion maturation and only IN tetramers can be targeted by both compounds, we hypothesize that the predominant form of IN in virions resides as a tetramer.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that both compounds are potent during virion maturation and both can target tetramers.

claim: IN tetramers bind viral RNA and are the essential building blocks for super molecular assembly of lentiviral intasomes.
source: It should also be noted that IN tetramers bind viral RNA and are the essential building blocks for super molecular assembly of lentiviral intasomes (Ballandras-Colas et al., 2017; Kessl et al., 2016; Passos et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published structural studies.

claim: Binding of functional IN tetramers to the viral RNA genome are important for effective packaging of these viral components within conical CA cores and formation of the infectious virions.
source: Collectively, our current findings together with published results (Kessl et al., 2016) suggest that binding of functional IN tetramers to the viral RNA genome are important for effective packaging of these viral components within conical CA cores and formation of the infectious virions (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings and published results, representing an inference about the mechanism.

claim: ALLINI treatment results in aggregation and separation of IN from RNPs, with both IN-ALLINI aggregates and RNPs lacking IN mislocalized outside of the protective CA cores yielding eccentric, non-infectious virions.
source: In contrast, ALLINI treatment results in aggregation and separation of IN from RNPs. As a result, both IN-ALLINI aggregates and RNPs lacking IN are mislocalized outside of the protective CA cores and yield eccentric, non-infectious virions (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on the current findings and published results, illustrated in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Combinations of ALLINIs and INSTIs exhibited additive or even synergetic effects to inhibit HIV-1 in cell culture.
source: It should also be noted that a previous study has shown that combinations of ALLINIs and INSTIs exhibited additive or even synergetic effects to inhibit HIV-1 in cell culture (Christ et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: There are potential clinical benefits of combining (-)-KF116 and DTG to treat HIV-1 infected patients.
source: Our observation that (-)-KF116 exhibits substantially enhanced, sub-nM activity with respect to DTG resistant HIV-1NL4-3(IN N155H/K156N/K211R/E212T) provides further support for potential clinical benefits of combining these two inhibitors to treat HIV-1 infected patients.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential clinical applications based on the in vitro data.
